extracted.intended_audience: aspiring fiction writers, especially short-story writers and creative-writing students
extracted.subtask_description: Practical craft advice for contemporary short-story writers on choosing subject matter, shaping endings, deciding about MFAs, and understanding literary appreciation. Focused on the short story form and the writer's perspective.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to figure out what to write about
rubrics_metrics.description: If you’re going to be a contemporary storyteller, you’re going to want to sort of pay attention to how these things intersect and what were on particular people’s minds or on fictional characters minds. Or what is on your own mind.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Write from the center — avoid writing about things that are not on your mind. A common mistake (especially among undergraduates) is to be 'off-center' and not truly care about the subject; instead, find what you personally care about and let disparate concerns converse in the story. Pay attention to intersections between personal concerns and social/character contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to write the ending of a short story
rubrics_metrics.description: There are ways of taking pivotal central moments that are actually earlier on chronologically and sticking them at the end. The end of a story is really everything. It gives the whole meaning to the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The story's ending need not be the chronological end; authors can pull a pivotal moment from earlier in the narrative and place it at the end to furnish the whole story with meaning. Treat the ending as the element that supplies or reframes the story's meaning.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why the ending of a short story is more important than the ending of a novel
rubrics_metrics.description: The ending of a novel sort of concludes the energies and looks forward and somehow you have a sense of what’s going to happen to these people... But the ending of a short story spins and looks back over the short story and so it’s more retrospective in a way.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because short stories are retrospective, it's effective to take pivotal moments from the middle and place them at the end; this irony — that what appears earlier to characters becomes the conclusion — creates interest and gives the short story its distinctive closure compared with a novel's forward-looking conclusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to decide whether or not to pursue an MFA in writing
rubrics_metrics.description: It’s just a café where you come to gather and you talk about literature and writing and compare notes. If you’ve got another café where you can do that, you can do it there. You should never go into debt for it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat an MFA primarily as a community and place to discuss literature; do not take on large student loans for it. Prefer programs that are inexpensive, low-residency, distance, or fully funded — examples cited include Wisconsin, Vanderbilt, Cornell, Texas, and Michigan, which fund students completely. If you have personal financial support, that changes the calculus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Why readers need life experience to fully appreciate certain writers
rubrics_metrics.description: You have to be able to sort of turn and look back at life, you have to have a sense of water under the bridge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appreciation of writers like Alice Munro and Chekhov often requires the ability to look back on life and recognize accumulated perspective and hindsight; youth may lack the 'water under the bridge' sense that deepens appreciation of such work.
